valuation_philosophy: Solution Dynamics is a net-cash micro-cap in the middle of a structural earnings reset, so the valuation hinges entirely on the NORMALIZED free cash flow of the business AFTER the loss of its largest international (aid-funded NGO) customer in mid-FY2025 — not on the elevated FY2023-FY2025 results that included that customer, and not on the depressed FY2026 trough year that is distorted by one-off restructuring. We anchor the base case on a normalized ~NZ$2.0m FCF (vs a 9-year median of ~NZ$2.8m and a FY2026 trough near zero), which is a deliberate haircut to the historical run-rate to reflect the permanently smaller revenue base. Net cash of ~NZ$8.4m (no debt) is roughly NZ$0.57/share — almost the entire current share price — so the market at NZ$0.58 is effectively assigning close to zero value to the operating business. The DCF instead values the operating business at a normalized mid-cycle level and adds back the cash. The large apparent upside is therefore a function of the market pricing the company near liquidation value while the model assumes the remaining business survives and stabilizes; the wide gap reflects genuine survival/execution uncertainty, which is loaded into a deliberately high ~17% WACC rather than into the cash flows.

historical_cagr.note: CAGRs computed on FY annual data. FY2026 is excluded from trend CAGRs because it is a structural step-down (loss of largest customer), not a continuation of the prior trend. These growth rates describe the PRE-reset business and are NOT used directly to project the post-reset base case.
historical_cagr.comment: Equity compounded ~18%/yr (retained earnings + buybacks net) while revenue grew only ~4%/yr and FCF was roughly flat-to-down, reflecting cash accumulation rather than operating growth. The FY2026 customer loss invalidates extrapolating any of these forward, so the base case is built bottom-up on a normalized FCF estimate.

wacc_rationale.explanation: Starts from a standard ~11.5% NZ small-cap WACC and adds explicit structural premiums: +2.0% for severe customer concentration (the largest customer just departed catastrophically and the top-5 still represent ~46% of revenue); +2.0% for micro-cap illiquidity (market cap ~NZ$8.5m, very thinly traded on the NZX); +1.0% for accelerating structural decline in physical mail volumes (NZ Post postage up ~44% in two years pushing clients to digital); +0.5% for management transition (Acting CEO since January 2026). The resulting ~17% discount rate is where the business-survival risk is captured, allowing the cash-flow assumptions themselves to remain at a plausible normalized level.

base.label: Base — normalized post-customer-loss steady state
base.fcf_assumption: Normalized FCF of NZ$2.0m: a smaller revenue base of ~NZ$30-32m at a ~10% EBITDA margin once restructuring settles, less tax and light maintenance capex. This is below the 9-year FCF median of ~NZ$2.8m to reflect the permanent loss of the NGO customer.
base.growth_rationale: Modest ~2.5% growth as digital/SaaS (nGAGE, council water billing) offsets ongoing physical mail decline — roughly tracking inflation/flat real volumes.

bull.label: Bull — nGAGE traction + Local Water Done Well pipeline
bull.fcf_assumption: Normalized FCF of NZ$2.5m: the remaining business stabilizes faster and new growth engines contribute.
bull.growth_rationale: nGAGE (AI-native product for UK dental corporate groups) scales beyond the first two signed groups, and NZ council water-entity reforms (Local Water Done Well) drive a multi-year pipeline of new billing-communications clients.

bear.label: Bear — continued attrition + accelerating mail decline
bear.fcf_assumption: Normalized FCF of NZ$1.5m and declining: further customer attrition among the concentrated top-5 and faster physical-mail erosion compress the NZ operation.
bear.growth_rationale: Revenue and FCF keep eroding before stabilizing at a lower base; new products fail to offset legacy decline.

base.method: Base terminal equity value per share (incl. net cash) discounted back 5 years at 15%

sensitivity.note: Base case intrinsic value per share across WACC (rows) and terminal growth (columns). Normalized FCF held at NZ$2.0m.

trip_reasons_considered: Base case upside 159.8% exceeds 100% — BUT the second condition (price in upper half of 10yr range) is NOT met: current price NZ$0.58 sits at the very BOTTOM of the NZ$0.56-3.26 range, so the market is pricing the BAD news, not the good. This condition does not trip.
Implied P/E 8.5x (FY25) / 15.3x (normalized) is BELOW the 10yr average of 17.4x — not a trip.
Implied P/B 1.96x is well below the 10yr average of 5.76x and below most historical years (only recent FY2025 traded lower at 0.78x) — not a trip.
Implied EV/EBITDA 4.6x on normalized EBITDA is BELOW the 10yr average of 8.0x — not a trip.
sanity_check.diagnosis: No peak-FCF extrapolation: the base year FCF (NZ$2.0m) is already a haircut to the 9yr median (NZ$2.8m) and well below the FY2023/FY2025 peaks (~NZ$4.2-4.6m). WACC is high (17%) with documented structural premiums. The large headline upside is a deep-value gap: the market values the company near net cash (EV ~ zero) on the view that the operating business may not survive, while the model assumes it stabilizes at a normalized level. Implied multiples are all below this company's own history.
sanity_check.fix_applied: None required — sanity check passes. The model was already built on normalized (not peak) FCF and a risk-loaded WACC. We deliberately set the base FCF at NZ$2.0m (below the NZ$2.8m median) and kept terminal growth at 2.0% to remain conservative.
sanity_check.investment_framing: This is NOT a multi-bagger growth thesis — it is a deep-value / asset-backed situation. Roughly NZ$0.57/share of the NZ$0.58 price is net cash, so downside is partially protected by the balance sheet while upside depends entirely on whether the remaining business can stabilize at a normalized FCF. The risk is a value trap: if the operating business keeps eroding (bear case) and cash is consumed, the asset backing degrades. Position sizing should reflect the micro-cap illiquidity and binary survival outcome.
